utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. There was a delay due to some technical difficulties. We have to be very efficient, in terms of time this week. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please start your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Excellencies. Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Ristanic.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to thank you for your kindness for agreeing to meet with the Defence, which I hope will facilitate this cross-examination and expedite it. I would like to ask you a few questions in relation to examination-in-chief. On page 60, it was stated and you agreed that the bridge had been blown up by the Serbian forces. Then on page 66, there was also a reference to the Serbian forces. Let us clarify one thing. Given that the Serbian forces feature in the pre-trial brief and the indictment as a unique entity that had unique control and single control, do you understand them as being composed of Serbs or the forces that were under the control of the Serbian authorities?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were primarily forces made up of the Serbs. But at the time when the bridge was blown up, that was the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So if we say "Serb forces," that does not mean that was a single formation under somebody's control, but, rather, we're referring to ethnic composition, and it would be necessary for each individual formation to establish the composition and the subject of control?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would be true at that time.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ristanic, can I remind you again that you need to put a pause before you start answering the question, because everything should be interpreted. Thank you, Mr. Ristanic. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 64, my learned friend the Prosecutor suggested that Brcko had been taken over. I would like to see a map so that we can see who has taken over what in Brcko, and from whom. As the man number 1 of the Serbian authority in Brcko, tell me whether there was any plan and preparations prior to the take-over of Brcko.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have a plan to take over Brcko. The only plan we had was that for the evacuation due east towards Bijeljina, or, rather, towards Serbian villages. That was what we referred to Alternative B, if I'm not wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you aware with similar recommendations on plans in the event of the outbreak of war? The plan was to save the population by taking them out to Serb-controlled areas, and I'm mean the population from Zenica, Tuzla, Gostovici, which is south of Zavidovici, and from Brcko. For the most part, the people left Zenica. Thanks to the kindness of the Croats from Gostovici, the people moved to Ozren, and it was very difficult for the remaining areas. Whereas in Brcko, due to certain circumstances, people remained behind; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct, but the Serbs left the town proper and moved to the Serbian villages located towards the Drina and eastwards of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Not towards the Drina, but it should be Bijeljina?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. You did not misspeak. It was wrongly recorded. On that same page, you said that there was shelling coming from both the north and the south. I'm afraid that it remained unclear as to who was positioned to the north of the Srpska Varos and north of the Srpska Varos, that is to say, the Serbian parts of Brcko, and who was it that was shelling these areas?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The River Sava is to the north, and across the Sava is the Republic of Croatia. To the south at the time, at a distance of up to one kilometre were the positions, what were then the Muslim Croatian forces. Therefore, the shelling sometimes came on Croatia, specifically Rajevo Selo, and more often from the southern part vis-a-vis the Srpska Varos, which was the Muslim municipality of Rahic, and it was renamed the free Brcko two days after the outbreak of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 66, there was a discussion about the civilians in the barracks. Were the civilians detained in the barracks, or did they find shelter with the JNA?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Initially, all of them found shelter there. The people who had been encircled within the radius of one or two kilometres, all of them decided to go to the barracks or to the Serbian village, Brezik, Stanovi, Razljevo, et cetera. And later on, they returned to the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were among them Serbs, Croats and Muslims who found shelter in the barracks?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were all ethnicities. I apologise. Yes, there were people from all ethnicities, and the ones from the other two ethnicities outnumbered the Serbs, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 68, there was discussion about passes, and it was said that a pass was issued to -- passes were issued to Jelisic for people he decided to let through. Could anyone who received this pass be deemed to be lucky?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know how to answer this question. These passes were issued in the Sumarija building at first, then in the police station and the garrison. Basically speaking, all the people received passes which allowed them to leave freely, with the exception of those who were detained. Now, speaking specifically about the passes given to Jelisic, I think that those people who received them were lucky.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So did the authorities need these passes or did the people who wanted to pass without any obstacles, without being treated as paramilitary, terrorists, et cetera, wanted them more?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the purpose of these passes was to ensure free movement, and it was valid along with an ID. It had to be shown to military forces that were manning check-points, and without any further checks they were left through.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And that certainly had to do with the front-line which was very close; right?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At the time, the front-line was at about 800 to 1 kilometres from the River Sava, so it was very close. It was practically within the town, itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 71, you said "he didn't listen to us." I didn't comprehend completely whether you referred to Veselic or Goran Jelisic, but what I'm more interested in is that it was recorded "he didn't listen to us." However, listening or obeying is important to make a distinction between. Did you mean that he wasn't listening to what you were saying or that he didn't obey what he was told to do?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant that he didn't obey.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you talking about Goran or Veselic; Goran Jelisic or Veselic?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's out of context, but I was primarily referring to Veselic, because with Jelisic, we didn't have any communication or control over whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please help me clarify another term that was used. On page 82, there was reference to the people killed or murdered. There is no distinction in the English language between these two terms. Can you help me clarify this for the Chamber? If you say in Serbian "got killed," does that imply the loss of life, unrelated to any criminal activity, that is to say, in combat or in accident?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you say "poginuli," in our language it implies that somebody was killed in combat in unrelated criminal activity; that is to say, by a shell, by a stray bullet, in their apartment, at the street, or on the front-line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, the same applies to those who lose their lives in accidents. Nobody says that they were "poginuli." However, if you say that somebody was killed, that implies some kind of criminal activity?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 84 and in document P2889, somebody from the military said that he was not very much bothered by your statement that a large number of people were killed. Do you agree that the army and the civilian authorities were not in agreement, that they were slandering each other?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. That was the case even before the conflict started in the former Yugoslavia. That was the kind of latent animosity that always existed between the army, primarily the officers, on the one hand, and the civilian authorities, on the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I read a portion of this document, where it says that not that you weren't bothered, but that you didn't feel responsible, and you distanced yourself because you didn't feel to have had any responsibility with regard to that?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with that document. It speaks about an intelligence officer from East Bosnia Corps. I first saw this document and heard of it some three or four years ago, when there was some local trials held in Brcko. I don't remember that man at all, nor any conversation with people of his kind, and I don't see any reason for the military to be observing us civilians and to give their interpretation of our conduct. Therefore, I believe that these are more some personal impressions that were not based on any proper conversation. In other words, there was no valid reason for any civilian to be bothered by that, as they put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 85, there was mention of contacts between Dr. Beli and the leadership at Pale. Since Dr. Beli spent most of his time during that period in Belgrade, is that an opinion of yourself, or, rather, wishful thinking that he was frequently in contact, or did it really happen?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: The reference to Dr. Beli spending most of his time in Belgrade, I think that's assuming a fact not in evidence. Or if it is, I would like to be pointed to that portion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in numerous statements, Mr. Ristanic persistently said, and he can confirm or deny that, that Beli spent most of his time in Belgrade, and that he only thought that he was in touch with Pale, but he didn't know that for sure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the conflict, it is true that Dr. Vojinovic or Dr. Beli spent quite a lot of time in Belgrade, and it is also true that I assumed that at the time, he was able to control [as interpreted] more or less frequently, but I have no reliable proof of that. I don't know if he did it on a daily basis or wherever he wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says "control." Did you say "control" or "contact"?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said "contact."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 86, there is a reference to thousands of people who got killed, and my appeal to President Bush to help us to shed light on this. Eventually, can we speak about 3.000 or fewer than 300? I am not saying that even three people is not horrible enough, but for the sake of the truth, can we establish the figure?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Officially, it is below 300. Initially, it was 8.000, then 6.000, then 3.000, and ultimately we arrived at the figure that I mentioned a minute ago. Unfortunately, that, in itself, is a big number too. In the first days of the conflict, there were hundreds of dead, but according to the media, such as Slobodno Brcko, they immediately started disseminating this kind of news, and this news reached international media and other sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: For a better understanding, Malo Cerakic [phoen], Slobodno Brcko, are all these pseudonyms for the Muslim Brcko and the Muslim-held territory?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is south of the town, and those were the pseudonyms for the Muslim municipality or the Muslim part of the town and the villages that are populated 100 per cent by Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On television, I saw a monument to the Serbs who lost their lives in Brcko. How many Serbs lost their lives in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number. But when we're talking about the total number involved, we have to see who were the civilians that got killed, that is to say, persons who did not take part in combat and who lost their lives in combat, on the other hand. I think that the brigade sustained losses. That 1st Bosnian Brigade sustained losses that amounted to 400. I'm not sure about other units from the Eastern Bosnia Corps and the 1st Krajina Corps and the 2nd Krajina Corps, and they were there every now and then. As regards civilians - please don't take my word for it, there is exact information about this - but I think that over 45 civilians got killed in town on account of the shelling that we spoke of at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Forty-five civilians," that was the word that you used. It was not recorded. That was the figure you received to?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I wasn't sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when the National Assembly was in session in Brcko, shelling took place and civilians lost their lives?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. I think the year was 1994, and I think that Brcko was shelled on that day, and I think that seven persons got killed. I'm not sure, but in the centre itself, about 100 metres away from the location where the Assembly was in session, an entire family got killed; a woman, her father, a child, and also a child that was not even born yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's clear the witness is talking about events in 1994. I'm wondering what the relevance is of this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I asked about the persons who got killed, but the fact remains that that was the attitude of the other side towards our Assembly. They were shelling us, whereas we gave safe passage and escort to their MPs. We have documents to prove that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are having very limited time, Mr. Karadzic. Please concentrate on the more relevant issues.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Excellency. I forgot it was 1994. However, I know it had to do with the session of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ristanic, on page 86, there is -- P3029, that is, it is being suggested that in October, there were camps as well. Until when did the Luka Camp exist in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could never give a precise answer to that question. I think that it was disbanded definitely sometime in June. I'm not sure, but I think -- I think it was the month of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Bearing in mind that you did not actually know at the time when it was established, and that it was only later that you found out what was happening in the camp, was there a way for the Presidency of Republika Srpska to have been informed in a timely fashion about details of what was going on in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At first, we thought that there would be some kind of co-ordination or whatever. But there was a great deal of difficulty involved, in terms of these contacts, and it was not only with the Presidency of the republic, but also for the police station, with the Ministry of the Interior. Telephone communications were not safe, and it was hard to make proper telephone calls. There weren't any special communications. So very often when you would even reach someone by phone, actually, you'd reach only the office. The man would not be there, himself. So very often this was discouraging. People were, in a way, discouraged from establishing contact with others. I think that there was a multitude of problems in all municipalities, because even larger organisations could not have managed so many problems during that short span of time. Of course, ultimately these problems were being resolved. I hope I was clear on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Am I right if I say that for the Serbs in Brcko, peace was their only chance, or fleeing towards Serb areas, and that it was only by way of peace and agreements that they could have had a municipality of their own and a safe life in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the assessment of the leadership, that quite simply we are a minor player, a minor force. There was hardly anything we could do. We could only survive in peace, or perhaps we could move out to safer areas, these Serb villages. But they had to be defended, too, in a way, regardless of where they were. Those areas had to be defended as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could I briefly paint a picture of the post-electoral situation, that is to say, which officials held important positions. Mustafa Ramic from the SDA, a Muslim, was he president of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The president of the Executive Board, was that Pero Markovic, and who was he?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Pero Markovic. He was a Serb, a member of the Serb Democratic Party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The chief of the Public Security Station, was that Stjepan Filipovic, and was Zlatko Jasarevic the commandeer? Jasarevic was a Muslim; Filipovic was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the MUP, did the Serbs have the position of the commandeer of the traffic police?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The commander of the Territorial Defence, was that a Serb, Milica [as interpreted] Milutinovic, who did not agree -- or, rather, who did his best to have the crisis overcome and to have the Territorial Defence remain as a single force?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It should also be said -- I apologise for interrupting. It should say Milisav Milutinovic, not Milica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I did say "Milisav ," but perhaps it wasn't clear enough. Thank you. Am I right if I say that the negotiations of the transformation of Brcko into three municipalities, every one of the municipalities had a part of the inner town and villages that belonged to that urban area?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would that have been a good solution, Mr. Ristanic, because Sarajevo has 10 municipalities, many other bigger towns have several municipalities?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in peacetime, that would not have been a problem at all. Three administrations that would have had, perhaps, something in common, I don't think that would have been a problem at all if everyone would have agreed to it at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about the city infrastructure? Would it have remained as it was, and schooling, cultural life, et cetera, would that focus on the ethnic communities?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that infrastructure would have to be joint infrastructure, waterworks, power, whatever else, but everything else would have been divided along ethnic lines, as is the case today in Bosnia, as far as culture is concerned and all of these other ethnic or national characteristics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement of 2003, on page 16, you said that it was impossible to do anything in secret and that the Crisis Staff could not do anything that would not have been made public.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sort of. It's a small community, generally speaking. There is a saying to the effect that we are like a torn sack, everything falls out. Once something had been agreed upon, it would leak one way or the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 65 ter 22238. This is for the participants. We don't need to call it up. We just need the participants to know where this is. On page 23 of that statement, there is a question, and they're asking you whether your estimate of the active and reserve policemen, Territorial Defence, Civilian Protection units, whether: [In English] "... being about the full letters necessary for the engagement." [Interpretation] Your answer: "Nothing was done, absolutely nothing." And then on that page, you explain that the Crisis Staff was not prepared for that. People were fleeing, all three ethnic groups. Everyone was fleeing. And this chief of the Territorial Defence said that he didn't want to command Serbs only.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do we agree -- actually, you say on that page as well that the JNA was there. Do we agree that that was a rather poorly-manned garrison, and in view of the experience gained in Croatia, this garrison lived in fear of a blockade and total annihilation?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you put it right. It was very poorly manned, in terms of active personnel, officers. And also, it was poor from the point of view of resources. It was called a motorised brigade, but I think they had one or two tanks only. And for the most part, they had infantry weapons. On the basis of the experience from Croatia, probably there was fear there, and there was constant threats that there would be a blockade of the barracks, that power would be cut, water supplies. Well, we took part in this tripartite government throughout, regardless of all the problems that were there, the many problems that were there, because we wanted to make sure that things functioned properly, and we did not want to have a situation like the one that they had in Croatia and everything that happened to the garrisons there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now that we're on the subject, perhaps it's best if I ask you now. Since the army, the reservists, the mobilised persons were looking at what the civilian authorities were doing, and if the civilian government withdrew, then they would flee as well: Did the JNA want to keep the authorities in the barracks, where they had put you up, in order to make sure that there were no further desertions?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly that was one of the stronger reasons for that. Any departure from town, any time certain individuals left town, people who were in power, I mean, prominent citizens, if we can put it that way, people would notice straight away and panic would prevail. I think that the garrison and its leadership had that attitude all the way up until the outbreak of the war. And this was rather successful with the Serbs, and with the Muslims to a degree, but very unsuccessful with the Croats, so it was an indicator that it was possible to discuss things, to have people stay on, to provide guarantees that nothing would happen, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How wide is the Sava River there, Mr. Ristanic?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, say 350 metres. I don't know. During the year, the average width is, say, 250 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So 250 metres away from town, the war had just ended between the JNA and Croatia; right? It went on for a few months, and it took a long time for things to calm down in 1992, isn't that right, after 1991?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Vukovar is 30 kilometres away, as the crow flies, and, of course, the war in Vukovar was finished by the end of November. But it took quite a long time for things to calm down, the area of Slavonia and Croatia, an so on, so it was felt for quite a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Not going into your actual knowledge as to who the authors of the papers known as Variants A and B were, on pages 14 through 20 of this statement and further on, you said that nothing or almost nothing was done on the basis of that paper. Did anyone ever call from SDS headquarters to ask for a report on the status or the state of affairs with regard to that paper? Did anyone ever ask you to apply certain things or did they ask you to report on the implementation?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never been asked any such thing, myself. I cannot confirm that anyone made phone calls and urged anything in that respect. Our assessment was that what can be done should be done, and what cannot be done should not be done by force. When I say "by force," I mean that we should not engage in exercises in futility. Some things were not even touched, some things were not completed, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you then agree that this document, unlike other party decisions, was optional, so those who wanted to could implement things, but those who did not want to would not be subject to any pressures or sanctions from the party?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, to be quite honest, I don't recall the document or the content. It probably did not contain anything referring to consequences of failure to implement it. It was part of a campaign, something to do with the plans of the European Union, Cutileiro, and so on. So what we did was look at what was agreed on at the top. If something was agreed on at the top, we would implement it. Otherwise, we wouldn't, because nothing could remain secret. Had we been preparing something in secret, it would have leaked out, so we refrained from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall, when you were drawing up the lists for the elections, did anyone from the SDS Central Office interfere in what you were doing or did you do this completely autonomously?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the Municipal Committee, we drew up the lists, ourselves. I think a list of some 90 persons was drawn up, and in the first 20 or so places, we put more prominent and better qualified people. So I don't recall anyone ever putting pressure on someone to appoint someone to this or that post, the way things are done today. We simply did things the way we wanted to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe that the interpreters want both of us to slow down and make more pauses, and it's in the interests of the Defence, because everything should enter the transcript. On page 30 of this statement, 22238, you say that events influenced the situation more than these instructions did because some sort of self-organising had already begun and everyone was cautious, and the war was just across the river, it was that close.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, because we saw what was happening in Croatia every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How far is Bosanski Brod away from Brcko, as the crow flies?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as the crow flies, not more than 50 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall that every incident was widely publicised and broadcast, and that very often soldiers from Croatia crossed the bridge, either the National Guard Corps, or some unidentified paramilitary units, or the regular Croatian Army, and together with Armin Pohar and the local Croatian and Muslim para-militaries, they killed people in Bosanski Brod? The first time they crossed the bridge was on the 3rd of March, and then on the 25th of March and the 26th of March in Sijekovac.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know the dates and names you mentioned, but everybody knew about the incursions of Croatian forces into Bosanski Brod, and especially the crimes in Sijekovac which are still under investigation, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you recall that the Croatian side destroyed the bridge at Gradiska and the one at Samac on their side at a time when they were afraid that the JNA would cross over from Bosnia into Croatia, and that in Brcko, when the JNA was afraid that the Croatian Army would cross over into Bosnia, the JNA destroyed the bridges ? So do you agree that bridges are destroyed by the side which fears that the other side might cross the bridge?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know that in general. But as for Gradiska, Samac and Orasje, where the bridge was destroyed sometime in October 1991, and also in Brcko, where that well-known bridge which we referred to as the footbridge which could take only up to five tonnes in weight, that they were destroyed on the Croatian side, and what was left could only be used by pedestrians and small vehicles, so that, in a way, they were afraid of a Croatian invasion in Bosnia. I assume that was the reason for the destruction of the bridges, because no one would wantonly destroy bridges of such importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Referring to the plebiscite at page 36 of this statement of 2003, you say that no one was opposed to the plebiscite of the Serbian people, and it took place without any incidents, and that, on the other hand, the Serbs did not cause any problems when the referenda were held among the Croatian and Muslim communities in February and March?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when it comes to Brcko, that's quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was voting by secret ballot, and was there any way to determine who was loyal and who voted for what, or was it really a secret ballot?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the Serbian Democratic Party carried out the plebiscite according to the electoral lists which had already been in place since 1990. It was really by secret ballot. You would take a ballot paper and go behind a screen, circle the answer you wanted, and drop the piece of paper into a box. So it was truly democratic, it was really by secret ballot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The media at that time were functioning, and there were many reports about shooting across the River Sava from Bosanska Kostajnica, Bosanska Dubica to Bosanski Samac. Gradiska was shelled in Brod, and then there was the attack on Kupres, the murders of over 50 Serbs at Kupres. All this took place before the 6th of April. How did you manage to keep peace in Brcko for a whole month after the outbreak of the war in Brod, Kupres and Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was an agreement within the party that we should approach those negotiations according to the instructions, that all three sides should negotiate, and we agreed not to raise tensions; for example, when there was voting in the Executive Board - that was the municipal government, that's what it was called at the time - or when there was out-voting in the Assembly which happened from time to time, this out-voting. But our policy was simply not to raise tensions and to create an atmosphere of tolerance. In view of our size and our strength, we had only 14 assemblymen in the local parliament. We had only two prime ministers. So, at any rate, it suited us that there should be peace. We did not want to provoke anything. We simply monitored the situation, and, in a way, we were buying peace, hoping that somebody else at a higher level would manage to negotiate something, and that in this way we would be able to avoid a conflict, because we knew that we would be sure to lose it. As for the other side and this third side, I don't know what their reasons were. I'm just telling you my impression about our reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Taking into account what you have just said, were you in a position to bang your fist on the table at meetings of the Assembly of Brcko Municipality?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to me, personally, or to all the representatives and members of the executive?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I am referring primarily to you, personally, because someone said that you are in a position to dictate the course of events and to bang your fist on the table. Was this an option?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I'm not that sort of person. I have never done that sort of thing in my life. And my next point is that we were not in a position to dictate to anyone, especially not in the way you describe, because this was always broadcast on television, there were always journalists present. In April, the last month, there was no chance of an incident occurring. I remember some joint statements and some individual statements we made for the public, trying to calm down the population, to encourage the population. This Court probably has these statements. If not, I recently found them somewhere. So the chances that this is true are very small, indeed, non-existent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You, like others, were called up as a reservist. Until when were you a reservist?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the reserve composition of that brigade until, I think it was, the 21st of December, 1991, and -- well, this means I was there for a full three months, which is the most you were able to stay away from your job, your professional job. I responded to the call-up, as did many others at the time, and I spent three months in the reserve composition in the garrison which was some 300 metres away from my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So in 1991, you did not go to the Municipal Assembly in uniform. In 1992, in April, did you attend Assembly sessions wearing a uniform and banging your fist on the table?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never, never. Not only did I not go to the Assembly in uniform, I never put on my uniform except during those three months.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As a reservist, a conscript, did you have a rank?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was a reserve officer of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would now like to ask you about the six strategic goals that you spoke about on page 40 of this statement made in 2003. Is it correct that except for the corridor and, possibly, access to the sea, we discussed all these strategic goals with the other two sides in Bosnia-Herzegovina peaceably, and were these strategic goals, for the most part, built into the Cutileiro Plan or, rather, the Lisbon Agreement?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was our understanding, that these strategic goals which appeared in a document form much later, but that all the points in -- contained in these strategic goals, that all this should be achieved in peaceable conditions, in peacetime, not in war and wartime conditions. In war, there are other rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. If we look at the first strategic goal, ethnic separation into separate entities, do you recall that this was something that the European Community offered us as a condition for us to accept the secession of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the existence of Bosnia-Herzegovina within its existing borders, and that we agreed to this?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember this was agreed to. I don't know what under conditions. You know that better than I do, so that you would know that. But I know that the leopard skin, as it was referred to, was offered and agreed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, thank you for mentioning the leopard skin. Do you agree that in peacetime, assuming that there would be no war, the territorial continuity of these constituent units was not necessary? For example, in Switzerland, which has a certain number of inhabitants, everyone can have their own canton. They have 30.000 inhabitants. Let me simplify.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'll answer that. I'm just waiting for the interpretation. I'm just waiting for the interpretation so that we are not told to make pauses. But please simplify.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In other words, do you agree that a corridor, as a necessity, emerged only in the course of the war; that in Banja Luka, 12 babies died because nobody wanted to deliver oxygen, that it was impossible to communicate, and that the corridor appeared as a strategic goal only because the war broke out, but it did not exist as a necessity before the war?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the corridor, as an idea, emerged only during the war. It proved to be necessary in the war. Until then, nobody mentioned it. We all know what the word "corridor" means. It appeared as a necessity. You mentioned the deaths of those 12 babies, and there was not just that. This corridor was needed for the proper functioning and life of most of the population west of the corridor and up to the corridor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You are a reserve officer. If, in some places, the corridor is only 800 metres wide, is it possible to use infantry weapons across the corridor?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was the situation we had in Brcko for almost 15 months, these 800 to 1.000 metres, so you could never go through the corridor in safety. There was an anecdote saying that the authorities stopped in Brcko only when they had a flat tyre. Everyone would drive through at great speed because it was simply unsafe. There were many incidents when people got killed in that corridor, and they were killed by infantry weapons, especially in the part near the River Sava.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that in the Cutileiro Plan and the Lisbon Agreement, it was envisaged for the Serbs to get something in Posavina, but that somehow in the area of Brcko, this communication line was severed and that that happened -- or, rather, that this was acceptable in peacetime?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember any details. All I know is we didn't get anything as a result of these negotiations. We were featuring nowhere. Our great problem was how to ensure the functioning of the municipality, itself. The municipality of Brcko was equally divided, in ethnic terms. We had Serbs on both sides, and the Croats were in the middle. Therefore, it was vitally important for us to establish links between these Serbian villages, and the only way to do that was through the town. Therefore, we were rather dissatisfied with the solution and we were looking for other ways of making passages, which led to some new researches and new negotiations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 40 of the statement, you explain why it was necessary to expand the corridor towards Majevica in order to reduce the danger from fire that the corridors were exposed to; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You would then expect the prime minister or the president of the republic to stop at Brcko and have a cup of coffee?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly, and that happened later, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that the whole Province 3 in the Cutileiro Plan, including Posavina and Brcko, was handed over mostly to the Croats, and that I gave my agreement in principle to that plan, although we failed to ensure the corridor, and then later on the people rejected that plan?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember us being very frustrated due to that, and - how shall I put it? - our morale was deflated concerning our participation in politics or war, because nobody was able to explain to us how could we live with some viaducts that we would have passage on the south or on the east, that various maps were being drawn at the time and they were brought to the government, and eventually we would rather happy that this plan failed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If I'm not wrong, the Vance-Owen Plan, the whole Province 3 was given to them. But what you're talking about is something that was included in the Stoltenberg Plans that included the so-called tea passages with viaducts, and that Brcko would be divided east and west of the railway tract. Do you remember these terms, viaduct, tea passages east and west of the railway tracks; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I remember that clearly. But, thank God, that didn't happen. And I'm talking about Brcko, because I'm thinking locally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't know how much you know about the Strategic Goal 3, which is surrounded by some kind of confusion. Our position was not to have a solid boundary on the Drina between the two worlds. Did you understand it the same way or in the way as suggested in the indictment between the two-Serbian state? And in the mind of our people, was the Drina boundary line between the east and the west, the Orthodox religion and Islam, or is it a link to Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You put it rightly. The term "soft boundary" was a term that was mentioned very often, maybe by somebody later, by some irresponsible people, but we never talked about two states. I think that "soft boundary" is a very good term. Now, speaking about us Serbs, we never perceived the Drina as a boundary between the two worlds, as you said, between two civilisations and two cultures. We always perceived it as a natural border, the river that is just passing there and that could always be crossed, and that people could live on both its banks without establishing some very strict reasons that would make this impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In other words, that you didn't have a strict border regime; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 45 of the statement, you speak about how and what the JNA held under its control, and that we reinforced their ranks by providing manpower, and that those units were not under our command and control. Do you agree that our able-bodied men, young men, were in the JNA and that they joined in greater numbers once the Serbs and Croats ceased to respond, whereas --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic please repeat the second part of his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, the interpreters couldn't follow the second part. And, most of all, please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that our able-bodied men, Serbs, pursuant to our recommendation, responded to JNA call-ups, while at the same time the Muslim and Croat able-bodied men were released from that obligation towards the JNA and were available to their respective ethnic communities for a possible participation in paramilitary units?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the Serbs are concerned, we pursued this kind of policy of instructing and directing all able-bodied Serbs to respond to call-ups in order to man the units that were low in numbers, although it wasn't very easy because there was a lack of manpower. As for the other two sides, they started boycotting the army and the Yugoslav idea, in general, although before that, they were in favour of that. We didn't understand that, where they ended up. There were various speculations about paramilitary formations being formed, and these were very serious speculations that were coming from reliable sources, that there was an indication of that happening. However, we in Brcko couldn't know that with any degree of certainty. Nobody could confirm that to us, so that we were unable to react to that. We believed that in view of the shared power and joint authorities, that this would be resolved. However, it seems that somebody was pulling those strings from the very top.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your 2011 statement, page 10, it is suggested in the question that some of the negotiations that -- 65 ter 23193, page 10. It is suggested that the S -- the S -- secret wish in these negotiations was for the town to be divided along ethnic lines. However, you said that that was an instruction, and I believe that that was enshrined in the Cutileiro Plan. Do you agree that this division along ethnic lines would be better suited for a transformation of the town into three municipalities based on ethnic principle, as suggested by Cutileiro, which applied to the whole of Bosnia; that is to say, to establish three entities based on ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that suited us completely. We wanted to define the territories in a certain way to divide the municipality, because we were thought that during peacetime, that was -- that would have functioned properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On pages 42 and 43 in the same statement, you speak about the events from the Second World War and that a large number of Serbs and Jews were either killed or expelled. Do you agree that those who had been expelled during the World War II could deem themselves to be fortunate because otherwise, if they stayed behind, they were killed?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Brcko was occupied in the Second World War practically from day one by the independent state of Croatia because Brcko was in the so-called Croatian Banovina. And virtually until the very last day of the war, it remained under occupation. There was never any other force entering the town in order to liberate it. All the Jews and the majority of Serbs who didn't escape were killed. And to this day, there is a monument on the bridge commemorating these killings. In other words, anyone who managed to leave was fortunate, and I can say that only a few families returned after the Second World War. They chose to remain where they went because probably they had some very bad experiences in the preceding period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just one more question before the break. Is it true that Orasje and Odzak fell after Berlin and Zagreb, that they managed to resist longer than these two cities?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, what relevance is there?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is just before the break in order to complete the picture of our history of our people there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wanted to let you know that there is some minor schedule change for today's sitting. Given that there's a delay by 15 minutes at the beginning, we'll be sitting, for the first session, until quarter to 11, and we'll have a half-an-hour break, and then we'll have another 90-minute session, i.e., quarter past 11.00 to quarter to 1:00, and after which, thanks to the indulgence of staff, we'll have today only a 45 minutes' break, after which we'll sit until 3.00, in order to keep the total time as usual. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence supports this. I didn't know that. That's why I made these digressions, because I thought that we were nearing the end of the first session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ristanic, is it true, and you spoke about this in your testimonies given in Bosnia-Herzegovina on page 74 -- that's 1D3899. Maybe we can call it up in e-court, 1D3899. And then on page 74, you speak about the coming of 16.000 people from Sandzak to settle there, and, in an artificial way, they made Serbs a minority in some parts of the town. Is it true that in this artificial manner, the ethnic make-up of Brcko was changed?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, in good measure, that's correct. That was back in the 1960s and 1970s, when there was a huge influx of people from the Sandzak. But that involved all the people who came from the Sandzak, both in Serbia and Montenegro. People came to settle from down there. And I must admit that this whole process extended as far as Osijek to the north, across the Sava. There are still these -- Dizdarusa, Suljagica Sokak, which are two major settlements, and I remember that those were the settlements created by those people back in the 1960s and 1970s. So over a period of 20 years, quite a few people came to live there, and one can deduce that's judging by their last names, by the documents where their places are birth are indicated and their personal numbers, et cetera. I have nothing against those people, but it's a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It wasn't recorded that you said, "I have nothing against those people, but it's a fact." Can this please be recorded. Is it right, you said that?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. That's what I said. I have nothing against those people who came to live there, but it's a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did that bring about, primarily, cultural tensions and, on the eve of the war, ethnic tensions as well?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for the most part, because people who had come there were from a different culture, they had different habits and customs, different lifestyles, et cetera. Now, with the emergence of new political parties, members of this ethnic community, the settlers, managed to secure for themselves an important place or became very much engaged in promoting the programme of the Party of Democratic Action.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In other words, they were more inclined towards extremism than the local population; right?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you could put it that way, although one should not generalise. However, the -- the fact remains that all of us from Posavina, the local people, Serbs, Croats and Muslims, are rather peace-loving, tolerant persons; whereas others who came from other areas, these are the Dinara types, as they are known, they are more incident prone, not to say more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the statement from 2003, that is 65 ter 22238, on page 13, you say that towards the end of December, from the 21st until the 23rd of December, 1991, you were elected president of the Serb Assembly, and that you had your first and last meeting when Munib Jusufovic and others asked you, at the cafeteria of the municipality, Where is your territory for that kind of municipality? You said that your answer was that, This was not based on a territorial principle, but that it is there to represent Serbs and be in charge of Serb affairs. As for the Assembly of the Serb People in Brcko, did you understand that as a replacement for the Chamber of Nations in the municipality, or is that what Jews have throughout our country, the Jewish municipality, that does not require the existence of a particular territory; simply, it is in charge of the affairs of that community?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could put it that way. At first, yes, that was our understanding of it, because the other two parties were not really opposed to that, that we have our own assembly, especially in peacetime. That was, roughly, how we understood it. Now, whether it was exactly as a Jewish community, as you have put it just now, or whatever, but it wasn't anything special. It wasn't a legislative assembly or something like that, or, as you put it, say, a chamber of nation, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the statement from 1998, on page 2, you also say that that municipality was a Serb assembly, not a municipality from a territorial point of view, and that it did not function until the war. 222 -- 222637 is the 65 ter number. That is your statement of 1998, and you call it the Serb assembly, not the Serb municipality of Brcko, and until the war it did not function. Do you agree from that point of view it served the purpose of a chamber of nations, as it were, and that Brcko was transformed -- or if Brcko had been transformed into three municipalities, then that assembly would have been the legitimate authority in the Serb municipality?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was said that it was not in session and it did not create any problems to the official legal Assembly where the representatives of all ethnic communities were. At the same time, when the three communities, the three municipalities were created then it started functioning. It is true that it didn't happen start straight away in full capacity, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the same statement, 22237, on pages 5 and 6, you say that the ethnic communities were discussing the possibility of having an administrative division of the municipality in order to avoid conflict, and you confirmed that the Serb side had the greatest interest in that because it was the weakest of all three. Once the conflict broke out, were three municipalities actually established, and where were the Croat and Muslim municipalities in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the same time. That is to say that this central authority fell apart on the 2nd of May. Everyone went their own way, and everyone established something in a certain way. So there was a Serb municipality of Brcko; there was the so-called Brcko Rahic or Slobodno Brcko, that is the Muslim one; and then Brcko Ravne, that is the Croat Brcko. So basically they functioned at the same time, practically three new municipalities with their respective territories.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree -- actually, in your statement of 2003, that is, 65 ter 22238, on pages 51 and 51, you were asked how and why these other two national parties agreed on talks aimed at transformation, when they didn't really have to, and you say, I cannot be sure that the SDS asked for separation, but this was an agreement reached between the parties. Does this correspond to your experience; namely, that the Serb side in Bosnia, as a constituent people, could have prevented the secession of Bosnia-Herzegovina from Yugoslavia by a certain veto, and that the Muslims and Croats needed our agreement for a secession, and that it is with that in mind that they agreed to these arrangements?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is clear that Serbs, Croats and Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina were all constituent peoples, and that, according to the Constitution, not a single people could be out-voted, especially with regard to matters regulated by the Constitution, and that would particularly be true in the case of important things like secession and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On that same statement, on pages 54 and 55, you were asked, yet again, about the corridor, and it was even stated that this position of yours was quite a headache. And you say that that's not the way you perceived it, and you say that in peacetime everything looked different. You say that, as a matter of fact, you had reached agreement to have another session with the Muslim and Croat sides. It was planned, but it did not actually happen, due to what followed.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would it be right now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break now for half an hour and resume at 11.15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could I now please have 0701 - that's the ERN number of this map I'd like to have displayed - up to 0739 and then the 18th map, the municipality of Brcko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you tell us the 65 ter number again, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm trying to find it, Excellency. But I'm afraid that this has never been called up as such, so I cannot see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're trying to find our way through this: Mr. Ristanic, you said in your statement of 1998, on page 7, that the Serbs were arming themselves by responding to the call-up for reservists, and then they returned with weapons. Let me ask you this: Do you remember - and since you were a reserve officer, you must know this - that before the war, when there were military exercises of reservists, that people took weapons home, uniforms, and many even took weapons?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. All of us military conscripts had uniforms issued to us, gas masks, and everything else that was needed, as you said, various types of equipment, and we took all of that home. And there were members of the armed forces that had these weapons with them. I cannot remember exactly now. It wasn't general practice, but that did happen. It could be called practice.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: I think the map Mr. Karadzic is referring to is 65 ter 19095.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very kind of you, Mr. Hayden. Let's try that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for this, let me ask you another question. I would like us to conclude by the end of this session. Witnesses testified here that different paramilitaries first showed up as regular volunteers, they were armed, equipped, and then when they get fed up with the front-line, they'd become urban renegades and commit crimes in urban areas. Is that your experience?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I think that that was even a rule. They didn't have weapons, or uniforms, or anything, so they came to local garrisons. They got armed there. They formally became members of different units, but then afterwards they became renegades in accordance with their own plans, if I can put it that way.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I now please ask for assistance to be given to Mr. Ristanic. Could he please be given an electronic pen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And, Mr. Ristanic, I would like to ask you to draw this for us, what those first days looked like, what the actual deployment was. Maybe you could use different colours. Or, actually, first, let me ask you to mark the separation line, the one that ran parallel to the Sava River.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean at the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The very beginning.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could this just be zoomed in, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us zoom in before the witness marks. Mr. Ristanic, could you just wait, without touching the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Where it says "Luka Camp," the inner-city, all of that.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I understand, but I just want to be very specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Will this do, Mr. Ristanic? Please wait.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just wait a moment. They have to activate the pen.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is east of this line?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croat and Muslim villages and areas, and also a part of town, of course, a part of town as well [marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did I misunderstand you? Are you referring to the east or west in relation to this line?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I do apologise. To the east are Serb villages, Serb villages; towards Bijeljina, that is. And towards the west and south are Croat and Muslim villages. And also to the west, there are two villages that are populated by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And this line that you drew, the full line, is that where the separation line was or the confrontation line, the front-line?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. Well, after all, this is the way it was, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you mark the Muslim municipality of Brcko and the Croat municipality of Brcko?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's the Croat area, right, marked by an "H," and the Muslim side marked by an "M"? Could you place an "S" in the Serb area?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And this is the way things were while the corridor was interrupted. For how long did this go on?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the interrupted corridor, the 8th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could you please put the date there and sign this?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did we hear what does this dotted line mean?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that that's going to be the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that this dotted line roughly corresponds to the extension of the corridor in the later period of war?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I roughly marked the area of the town, itself, here, the urban area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Your signature, please, Mr. Ristanic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, this will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1570, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'd now like to ask you to keep this same map. This is going to be admitted, but then we're going to have a clean map. And then could you mark the establishment of communication with Posavina and Croatia, and also by the Sava River, what the corridor looked like?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the corridor was opened?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: For most of the war, did this remain like that, except near Brod? Can you draw a dotted line showing to what extent the corridor was widened in the direction of Brod in the course of the war?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did we ever control the streets?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When was this corridor broadened; in 1993?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1993, the corridor was broadened near Brod. There was a plant there that was necessary for the electricity supply, and then it was also extended to cover the streets. There are a few small places -- or, rather, not the streets, but a Croatian village called Ulice. There were some other small villages, such as Lucice [phoen], Donji, Gornji, and others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Can you put the date and your signature?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the blank map again without any markings?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This one will be admitted as Exhibit D1571.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now look at the unmarked map, and show us how, according to those negotiations and agreements, the cake would be cut up where every ethnic community would have parts of the town, the country-side, and so on? The Serbian area would remain more or less as it was; right?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will mark what we more or less agreed on by the end of April 1992. There were some small areas in the centre of town that had yet to be negotiated, but what we agreed on was the following. I'll mark it now. This is the Brka River Valley [marks], and we had two enclaves, two Serb enclaves [marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And this would be the Serbian municipality of Brcko, and the others would be Croatian and Serbian, and both would actually go into the centre of town?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you just draw a line between the Croatian and Muslim municipalities?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they didn't have much to say about that because there were no mixed villages. The Croats lived mostly in a few large villages near Brcko. There were not many of them, about three and a half thousand in the town itself, so that it was understood that the Croatian municipality would be composed of those Croatian villages. And this later came to be called Brcko Ravno. I will now mark it approximately [marks]. I forgot another Serb village here in this part [marks], and this is Bukvik [marks] which I mentioned. And, approximately, these would be the Croats [marks]. If this is all right [marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just tell me, is this Bukvik which was encircled by them and which was completed destroyed, and large numbers of civilians were captured and killed?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Bukvik and Cerik [Realtime transcript read in error "Serik"]. When I say "Bukvik," it's more than one village, Bukvik; Vujicici, Dzigure, Bukovac, I think six or seven hamlets which made up the Bukvik Plateau. This was on an elevated area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please put the date on this map and sign it, and then we'll look at another document.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May this be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Exhibit D1572.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now look at 1D3868.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In September 1992, Bukvik was liquidated; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have a telegram from you to the Presidency of the Republic and the Main Staff, and the commands of the East Bosnia and 1st Krajina Corps. Do you remember that at that time you were crying out, saying that in the area of Donji and Gornji Bukvik, 2.000 Serb inhabitants lived in encirclement, without any food or supplies, and that a hundred had already lost their lives, that they were completely encircled without food, ammunition or health-care? Do you remember sending this telegram?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: This relates to events in September 1992 concerning Bukvik. I don't see the relevance of this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may respond to that. These were enclaves which were immediately surrounded in April and May 1992 and were not a threat to anyone, and they were surrounded. We were not allowed to send them food supplies, and finally in September, they were liquidated. And to get a picture of Brcko as a whole, I think this is important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before that, Mr. Hayden, could you expand on the reason why you think this is not relevant?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: I understand that this document concerns alleged crimes against Serbs who are living in Bukvik in September 1992. I don't see how that relates to the crimes charged in the indictment, in particular the crimes charged in the indictment relating to Brcko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What did you mean by "the crimes charged in the indictment, in particular the crimes charged in the indictment relating to Brcko"?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Well, Luka Camp is the only crime charged in the indictment relating specifically to Brcko geographically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And taking over municipalities includes Brcko, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Clearly, we led evidence relating to the take-over of Brcko insofar as it relates to who was responsible for the crimes at Luka Camp. But the only crime in the indictment relating to Brcko is Luka Camp. The remaining crimes were not charged and were removed at the 73 bis stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And his evidence, written evidence, contains matters other than the Luka Camp itself?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: His written evidence goes wider than Luka Camp, but the relevance of that is establishing responsible for Luka Camp. So the evidence in his statement concerning Variant A and B instructions and the take-over of Brcko municipality is either direct or circumstantial evidence relating to who is responsible for the establishment of Luka Camp, and evidence subsequent to that temporally relates to notice concerning Luka Camp and responsibility for Luka Camp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While the Chamber doubts the relevance of this line of questions, but it may be helpful to understand the background at the end of the day, we allow the question to be put, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct, Mr. Ristanic, that as early as in May, when the conflict broke out, these villages were surrounded by hostile forces and that you had no contact with them, that you were unable to send them supplies of food and medicines; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when it comes to Bukvik. But as for Cerik and Bosanska Bijela, Cerik was immediately taken over - I think it was in May - by the Croatian and Muslim army, and the entire population expelled. The village was looted and burned down. Bosanska Bijela was a majority Croat village, but it did have about one-third of Serb inhabitants and the same thing happened to them. As for Bukvik, it remained surrounded in May, June, July and August, without any contact with the outside world, except for occasional contacts through the Croatian side which made it possible for meals to be delivered and some small matters like that. We had no control over the population in that area, and we could do nothing to help them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But you felt a certain responsibility and concern for them?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. They were members of our nation. They were in trouble. They had no water, no electricity, no food, no medicine. They used whatever they had over those four months.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for the record, "Serika" is written with a "C," not with an "S."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Those who managed to escape as refugees to the Serb part of Brcko, did they make the situation in Brcko worse, in economic and psychological terms?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were a burden for the civilian authorities in town for several reasons. First of all, they were constantly demanding that their fellow villagers who had been left behind be helped, and they were also looking for accommodation in the town itself. And they would often break into other people's houses which they thought should be theirs. There were even incidents when they expelled local Muslims from their homes so that they could move in. The situation was very difficult, and it was a great burden for all of us who were there in the town. So we had refugees and displaced persons from the municipality of Brcko, people from Cerik and Bijela who were already in the town. Then we had those who managed to break through the encirclement, a few families, and there were also people from other areas such as Smoluca, Bosanski Brod, and so on, refugees who had already been put up in the town. We had to provide for all of them, and it's well known that there was no electricity in town over those four or five months and we were short of everything. So it was very complicated, very difficult to prevent an outbreak of disease, to bring in water. When you have a situation where you have thousands of refrigerators and freezers left without electricity in abandoned houses, this all had to be cleaned up to prevent an outbreak of disease. We had about 10.000 refugees at one point. We had to provide accommodation for all of them. The army wanted to mobilise all those people, but they all tried to evade the call-up. So the situation was extremely confused, and there was constant pressure to help their people who had been left behind in Bukvik, either to get them out or to establish communication with them.
