This was a great burden. Many matters were pushed aside so that these issues could be dealt with on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And was there a threat of individual incidents of revenge by these unfortunate people who had lost family members and so on?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were such incidents. I can't describe any particular incident right now, but some were quite serious, especially after the fall of Bukvik. That gave rise to enormous problems.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May this document be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Now I understand that you will come to the real issues.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1573, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ristanic, conflicts were avoided. The army put you up first in a barracks, then in a village. Then you came back to the town. And in this statement of 1998, you were asked whether the War Presidency of the municipality could manage or control the police. This was in 22237, on pages 14 and 15. In your response, you said that you could not control the police, but that you could talk to the chief of police, who was a member of the War Presidency. Did you want to say that even under those conditions, it was the MUP which controlled the police, not the civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, at that time the Ministry of the Interior Affairs had not yet been established, it wasn't yet functioning properly, especially in Brcko. You have to know that when the bridges fell and the conflict broke out, the police station was abandoned. The Muslim and the Croatian officers left the police station and took with them all the cars and equipment. All that was left was an empty building with tables and chairs. We had only the building, and we were willing to establish a police force. There were some dozen active-duty policemen left and some reserve police officers who we managed to gather, but we could not actually manage what was going on in the police station. We could only make suggestions. We found it difficult to cope in that situation. I have to say that in the police station, there were one or two men who belonged to -- well, they were practically soldiers, but they were at the police station, acting as supervisors of a kind. They were exercising control. They couldn't be thrown out. And it was very difficult to clean up the police station from these intruders, and that's what the situation was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On this same page, you speak about the paramilitary and the supervisors, and you say that they even beat and arrested the Public Security Station chief. You even say that you, yourself, were arrested and that the civilian authorities in Brcko was suspended altogether at the time. You didn't use this particular term, but you can find it in other documents.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true, and that did not only involve the chief. There were people who wanted to establish some semblance of control, but, however, when those soldiers appeared, they would create problems. They, on two occasions, slapped the chief on the face, and then it escalated in July when a unit arrived in order to help. That was the time when I and the chief of the brigade were arrested. So there was a whole host of problems, and I really don't know how we managed to survive. After that, things slightly improved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We have to slow down and make pauses, and try to speak as slower as possible. Now, this increased number of reserve police officers, between 50 and 100 or maybe even 200, can one say that this surplus was actually a sort of deserters in disguise who, under the protection of the paramilitary, evaded going to the military and to the front-line?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the police work at the time was easier. That was the case until a problem would arise, because, then in May, all of them were sent to the front-line and the police forces were re-subordinated to the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. According to your experience and what we can see from police reports, whenever they purged the police, they would send them back to war units of the former JNA and later of the Army of Republika Srpska because they were not suitable for police work?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we discussed earlier, that was the result of this kind of rift between the military and the civilian authorities, and we can consider police to be part of civilian authorities. As soon as law and order were restored, and when the police stations started working properly and the curfew was introduced, an incident sparked, and I think that a crisis was virtually invented in order to send those people to the army, whereas at the same time members of the military were just walking around without getting involved in combat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 109 of the 2003 statement - it's 22238 - you confirmed that the most powerful force in Brcko were paramilitary formations. Do you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the very beginning and in town proper. As far as the line -- the front-line, as we called it, was confirmed, there were no paramilitaries there. They mainly operated inside the town, behind the backs of combatants, and in a certain way, never mind how they represented themselves, they were causing problems and exerting pressure on the authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you were pushed aside by the JNA. Then you were returned to the town. And from that moment on, you heard that a portion of the population -- or, rather, that some people were detained at Luka. This is what you heard some two or three days after your return. You heard about this prison in Luka. Is it true that at that time, you didn't know who set up the Luka Camp?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, nobody came for work and said, We establish this. Everybody was trying to lay the blame on somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that some people who found shelter in the barracks left in various directions, and is it true that among the detainees, there were also Muslim combatants and Croatian combatants, and is it true that they had been brought there, according to some rumours, due to their possible engagement?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, that was an excuse for setting up the camp. Allegedly, they found people having arrived for a sniper rifle, or knew that somebody was a member of Green Berets or had undergone training. So we heard such stories about quite a few people who were camped in the camp for those reasons. Now, whether that was true or not, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that there were stories circulating around, and maybe it was true, that the SDA had sent people from Brcko to be trained by the MUP of Croatia and that were also people from Brcko in the National Guard Corps of Croatia and other Croatian units during the war in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was a story that was being told around town for a long time. When the war in Croatia ended in November or December 1991, there was information and education, particularly when it came to people from villages. Everybody knew that they had been involved in fighting and they then came back. However, these things could not be verified and checked. These were stories, and that some formations had been trained in Croatia, formations made up of Muslim and Croats. In contacts with the Military Counter-Intelligence Service, it just happened that in 1991, I, myself, heard some information, because at the same time I was in the reserve force and I knew people from those circles, from the Counter-Intelligence Military Service. I heard, since they infiltrated the communities of the Serbs, the Croats and the Muslims equally, they had information to that effect. And, you know, these people from counter-intelligence services did not trust us Serbs either, so incidentally I heard about certain formations that were in the process of being established, composed of men who had undergone training. I can't give you any specific names, but they probably can. When I say "they," I'm referring to the former Counter-Intelligence Service of the Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your testimony in Bosnia on pages 88 and 51, in response to a question whether these units were seldom involved in war operations - that's 1D3899 - and that they exerted pressure on the Public Security Station, and that they even had an ambition to establish their own stations, you said that that could have involved the execution of certain people. On page 119, you even said that they wanted to have their own stamp to act totally independently, to have their petty cash, to have their bank account, that they organised the work of the police station, and to influence the political leadership, in terms of total control, and there were attacks on the Public Security Station?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, that is correct, and that was a major problem. For the whole of these three months, we struggled with those problems. The pressure was enormous. They wanted to draw us into this whole story, and that involved us civilians, first of all. But we did not help that in any way whatsoever. We always directed them and referred them to first the JNA and later the Army of Republika Srpska. Their ambition was that unless they cannot take part in managing all the affairs, to at least have some of their people installed in police structures and probably army structures and, of course, civilian structures.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your 1998 statement, 22237, on pages 21 and 22, you say that it was impossible to establish who set up the camp. Unlike collection centres in the Barracks Lazare, and transportation company and elsewhere, where the refugees found shelter, who, unlike those centres, set up the prison in Luka? You say that although it was impossible to determine who it was, it was clear that somebody did that?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Despite our persistent requests for identifying the persons running the show behind the scenes, we could not get this information. The people from the military pretended not to know anything about that. They said that they were completely uninformed. So it was a kind of vicious circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In 2003, statement 22238, on page 58 - I'm going to read the question in English: [In English] "Did the SDS Brcko support these red berets, these training officers, if you like, these red berets, or, in any way, logistically, or for funding, or through salaries, or staff like that?" "Ristanic: No, for us, they didn't exist before the war. That was strictly a military unit under the command of JNA. They had nothing to do with us. They were not our people, so we did not have reason to be satisfied or not satisfied." [Interpretation] And then on page 59, it's also being confirmed that they were not members of your party. They were Serbs, though, but you say the SDS was not the only entity in charge of Serbs, so you cannot equate the SDS with the Serbs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 118 of the same statement, you say the following --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: I can't find the reference to the passage Mr. Karadzic was just reading out. Perhaps the page numbers are not correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: 59, I suppose. The question was: "When you say they weren't our people, you were referring to the trainers, themselves? When you say 'they weren't our people,' who do you refer to?" "Ristanic: They were not members of our party.' "Q. Who wasn't a member of your party?" "Ristanic: Those people who participated in the training."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Have you found the page?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Page 56, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: E-court page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to have this document in B/C/S. The only version I have in front of me is in English. Could that be done, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: There isn't a B/C/S transcript of the 2003 interview.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With your leave, I am then going to read it out: [In English] "Right, but they were Serbs." "Ristanic: But SDS wasn't the only one in charge of Serbs. And you cannot put the sign of equality between all Serbs and SDS."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is that your view?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then on page 118: [In English] "Ristanic: It's only a matter of fear and cowardice. It is one thing that is very important at that time. The people from Red Berets controlled that police station in every aspect. They were the actual supervisors for the police because they -- of their will. Whenever we were trying to do something, they would make a mess in town. They would beat --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we have that passage? What's the actual page or e-court page? What do you have, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have page 118. It needn't be the same page in e-court; maybe one before or after that. Maybe it's a page after that. I'm going to be tendering this entire statement, so then perhaps it will be easier. Two pages down, perhaps. 117, maybe. Mr. Stojanovic will find that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The question of fear and cowardice, are you trying to say that there was no one in Brcko who could have opposed these men?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now I'm going to read out to you what a victim stated. That is 1D3890, paragraph 41, on page 14: [In English] "Both the prisoners and the guards equally feared Goran. Whenever Goran entered the camp, the guards scurried away like mice from a cat. Goran was the main man and did whatever he wanted." [Interpretation] As for your experience with Goran Jelisic, was it like this, that even guards had to run away from him like mice from a cat?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that, but I know that everyone avoided any kind of contact with him. How do I put this? Being so arrogant and being on your own, that was quite illogical, so people did not know -- actually, maybe if he were on his own, maybe somebody would have stood up to him. But it was a big secret, who was actually standing behind him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just a moment, please. You say that some people were released, and you said that you managed, in a way, through Veselic to send investigators, police inspectors, to Luka and to start working there; right?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did that result in an increased number of releases from Luka?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did these inspectors manage to talk to a considerable number of these detainees?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so. That's why they were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We had a witness here who was not protected, Gasi, who had spent 10 days in that camp. He was released with the help of some Serbs who belonged to Captain Dragan. On two occasions, he was told that he was there by mistake, once when he was taken out and the second time they said that it seemed that the Serb police had made a mistake. Were there such cases when they were looking for one person and then they would capture the wrong person by mistake? Do you have any such knowledge?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't, I really don't.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 118 a moment ago was actually 111 and 112, when Mr. Ristanic says that this was a question of fear and cowardice, and that was important, and these people had the police station under their control as well in every way. 22238, page 111 and 112. Yes, we have it: [In English] "It's only a matter fear and cowardice." [Interpretation] And then the next page, please. The rest is on the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Further on in your statement of 1998, you say, on page 22, that is, 65 ter 22237 -- we don't need to call it up. Everybody can have a look at that. You say that you did not know Jelisic personally and that you did not have any communication with him, but you do remember that he was in some escort when you toured villages. Was he a regular policeman or did he squeeze his way through into the reserve police corps that came into being as they fled from the front-line?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not a regular policeman. You know, at the time people came with all sorts of uniforms. They put rank insignia on them and this and that. People were trying to represent themselves in different ways. They were -- there were some people who were not actually in the police, but who were sort of messing around some check-points and whatever. But as for him, I do not know --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not understand the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat your last sentence, where you started: "But as for him, I do not know --" The interpreters couldn't understand the remainder of your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As for him, he certainly was not a policeman, not a regular policeman.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you say that you do not know how he managed to get into the ranks of the reserve police?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that in that context. There were many who came with different kinds of uniforms, most of them police uniforms, and they incorporated themselves in all of that. And as I said, some people were at the police station, others were freelancers, and so on and so forth. I really don't know how he found his way there. Later on, I mean, it's only important if you know something at that point in time. Everything I learned five or ten years later is irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But at the time, it's not only that you did not know how come he was there, but you also did not know -- or, rather, could you have known what was going on in the prison, itself, except for rumours and fears? Could one know, could one have insight into what was going on there?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the most part, these were rumours, when people went there to try to get someone out, and so on and so forth. However, specifically, officially, no, up until the very end, almost. We heard that they were mistreating them, in the sense of forcing them to sing, and so on and so forth. That could be heard from time to time, but we learned only later about what was going on there. Even to this day, I do not know how many people lost their lives in Luka, itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Then you found out -- or, rather, did you find out -- no, or you did find out that a group of special forces people was coming and that they were supposed to take care of the situation. Did you learn that that was at my request, sent to Milan Panic, prime minister of Yugoslavia? I had requested that we be assisted in resolving these crimes and problems related to the paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had this information from a person who had come with these men, that this person was sent by the federal government at your request. I was pleased because we were sending requests to the top leadership, and once and for all we would get rid of these people and everything that was going on by virtue of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement of 2011, on page 24 you say that problems in the police were -- you're actually explaining what kind of problems investigators had in the police from the fifth line onwards. There was no police station, basically, and later on it was established, and the process was a very slow one, that this was impeded by those persons with different berets. Actually, these berets, were they self-imposed or was this an official group? Had they abandoned the ranks of the army? Had they joined the urban forces? What was your understanding of these berets?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, look, formerly they were members of the military, in general terms. As for all of these troublesome persons, we call them the Red Berets. The vast majority of them were honourable and good men, but obviously this "Red Beret" was a kind of synonym for an elite unit. You know what the times were like. Whoever had an American uniform and a red beret was a big fighter, and there was no substance there whatsoever. Many who were not fighters at all joined these units. They were there in the army, and then they acted independently. They wore these berets. And when I say "independently," I'm not referring to individuals, just one or two individuals. Usually, these were groups that had a stronghold within the army, itself, because they played a double game. So this red beret, this cap, it didn't mean anything, ultimately. But to all of us, when we spoke about paramilitaries, we said it was the Red Berets, but formally we did not have a unit called the Red Berets in Brcko.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement of 2011, on page 23, you say that this late Veselic -- actually, the question says in the previous interview you said that it was necessary to have Veselic dismissed. I cannot really see it here. And you say that it was only the minister who could have dismissed him; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. The day that he got a decision from the Ministry of the Interior, he fell under the jurisdiction of the ministry, so, practically, we could make proposals to that effect, but it was the minister of the interior who had the final say or, rather, the chief of the Security Services Centre, that was the higher level, and then came the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have 65ter 8467 briefly, please. The Brcko Public Security Station, the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. That means that it was the month of July, at the latest, or the first week of August. I hope that there is a translation, too. It says here that the Public Security Station employed 86 operatives before the bridges were destroyed, and then the station stopped working because only a few employees reported for work. And that went on until the Territorial Defence took over the station.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was that the way it was?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that's the way it was. I don't know. As for this number, well, that would be it, roughly, because in peacetime there were about 100 people there, 120, 130. Eighty were policemen, and all the rest were administrative staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It says here that a small number of Serb employees were asked to come in to establish a proper police station. Did the Muslims and the Croats do that, and Rahic and -- what was the other one called?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Brcko Ravne. As far as I know, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the third third, it says that it was very obvious that they were poorly equipped and poorly trained, and that reserve police officers were often found on the front-lines; that is to say, they were often on the front-line, itself. And it says so far, especially during the first days of the operation at the Public Security Station, there was a serious number of persons present who were introducing themselves as inspectors, chiefs, et cetera, and that that created a problem. Also, they treated the employees of the public station in a brazen manner, and in this way they wanted to provide scope for realising their true intentions; robbery, and so on and so forth. Is that your view as well?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we have the next page, because we need to see the certification as well. [In English] Next page, please. The previous in English -- or next in English. [Interpretation] The next one in Serbian too. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see here that a proposal is being made, in terms of measures aimed at reinforcing the Public Security Station, reorganisation of management, appointment of new chiefs, with a view to improving discipline and sense of responsibility, to remove all persons from the reserve police who have been earlier charged with criminal acts, and cancel all unauthorised positions and assign persons who have the proper training for certain jobs, to get full support by the War Presidency and assistance to the station's management for the realisation of the mentioned and other planned measures? And further on, it says that: "In order to lift the operative activities to a higher level and to remove self-appointed inspectors, appropriate measures for improvement of co-operation with military security, neighbouring SJBs and the MUP of Serbia should be taken." Are you aware of this set of measures that was proposed?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen this document so far, but it's a fact that that's the way it was. I don't know when this document was drafted, but I remember some things in it. I remember we were asked to withdraw the police from the security. They were securing the municipal building, the post office, and so on. I remember that. And I mostly agree with this, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May it be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1574, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then Mr. Milorad Davidovic turned up with a group of some 15 specially-trained special officers in Brcko, special police officers. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 26 of the statement from 2011, you talk about this from line 8 forward, and that's 65 ter 23193. And page 26, you say you didn't have enough equipment: "We were constantly getting promises that this would be resolved step by step. And what happened in the end -- which in the end happened, but not under the Veselic's administration. It was, rather, a chain of circumstances, because a special headed by Mico Davidovic, who came to Brcko." Are you referring to Bijeljina or Zvornik when you say that he was doing something?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was from him I heard about Zvornik. But as for Bijevci [as interpreted], they -- as for the people of Bijeljina, they resisted his attempts to do something. But in Zvornik, he arrested the Yellow Wasps, or at least that's what he said. I don't know how much truth there is in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So that very soon, some ringleaders of these paramilitary units were arrested. Do you remember that event? You were at a meeting after which, in front of the municipal building, there was an arrest?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in front of the police building, because Assemblyman Vojinovic and I were attending a meeting at the police station in late July or maybe early August - I can't be sure - and suddenly a man burst in. I happened to know him because although we didn't know each other personally, I knew him by sight, because he was a policeman and he was married to my wife's sister. They -- he was at -- attended a Police Academy with somebody I knew. So then I realised who this man might be, and he said that he had been sent there to bring in some order. And I and the late Vojinovic were very happy to hear this. We left and went back to the Forestry, this building, where we were accommodated. And at that point in time, a van arrived. It was only later that we found out what happened. Then they went out, met two or three local members of the so-called Red Berets, and they came to ask them what they were doing there. An argument broke out. They arrested those men. They were beaten up and locked up, and then they left for Bijeljina. We didn't know all those details, but there was a lot of fear in the air, fear that a conflict might break out. I said that I wouldn't go to Bijeljina, that I would stay there, even at the cost of my life, because I wanted to solve, once and for all, this problem of the police station and people being maltreated. And Vojinovic said to me, Well, they'll beat you up. And I said, Well, whatever will be will be. And then two members of those Red Berets - and I use the term conditionally only because they were wearing red berets on their heads - they burst into the Forestry building, pointing their automatic rifles at us, and they asked for me. There were four of us inside at the time. And I said, I'm the one you're looking for. And they said, We have been ordered to bring you in to the police station. I asked, Why? They said, We don't know. Those are our orders. I wanted to use my car but they wouldn't let me. They --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please slow down so that every word enters the transcript?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I then asked my secretary, since there was no one I could call and the garrison commander was absent on that day - he was attending a funeral, so we couldn't turn to him - so I said, Please call the local priest and tell him I've been taken away. Let him try to use his authority. Let him come there and try to dissuade these people from any dishonourable intentions. On the road, I came across another member of the War Presidency. He was the president of the High Court in Bijeljina. He asked me where I was going, and I said, Well, you see I've been arrested. I don't know why. Maybe they think I stole something. Would you come with me? And he came with me. He said he would. He came with me. And for some 600 metres, we were conducted through the town with rifle barrels pointed at our backs. We were brought to the plateau in front of the police station, where there was some 200 or 300 men, well armed, wearing various uniforms and various colours of berets. There was a self-propelled machine-gun, a sort of smaller tank, and suddenly there were some screaming and yelling as if they had captured an important commander on the Muslim side, and then they wanted to lynch us. And we were lucky, because among these men there were two or three who knew us well and prevented the lynching. We were taken into the police station, and there we came across a duty officer who was in a small office -- or, rather, we saw that the chief of staff of the brigade had also been locked up there. And I saw members of those berets - and, again, I use the term conditionally - who were walking around, and they were very angry because their men had been arrested. They wanted to execute us. I asked them why they had arrested us, and they said, You will be hostages until our brothers are released. I asked the chief of staff, I said, Well, Milorad, what are you doing here? I'm not important, but how come you're here? These are men from the 1st Bosnian Brigade. And then I saw in the lobby battalion commanders who were local Serbs arriving. They were members of the 1st Posavina Brigade, and they didn't pay any attention to us. I found all this very suspicious, so I asked those men who were pointing their rifles at us whether I could use the phone. And they said, Yes. So I called up a Colonel Ilic, the chief of staff in Bijeljina, who said there was nothing he could do to help us. And I saw that we had been sacrificed or perhaps that we were simply pawns in somebody's game. The commander was absent, the commandeer had been beaten up and arrested. Others had been beaten up and arrested. So I broke off the conversation and I insisted on negotiating with Mico Davidovic. And then they -- some 20 kilometres away out of town, they met him, and they said they were going to kill us all. And he said, You can kill them all, but you won't leave the town alive. He gave them a dead-line. He said they had to leave town by noon the next day. I didn't know what they had said in that conversation, but I understood by their actions that the negotiations had been in our favour, not theirs. I asked whether we would be set free, and they said, Yes, yes, you will be released. And then I left town and went to Bijeljina. I removed myself from that place. And when I came back in the meantime, they had left, and then the situation calmed down. This was when the corps of that unit was broken up. The unit -- or, rather, the -- or, rather, individuals from that unit had been responsible for the problems. And then I met a cousin of mine, and I asked him, Why did you come to the police station when you were deployed on the front-line? And he said, Well, they came to us and they said that the people of Bijeljina had taken over the police station. And I said, Yes, well, they are members of our people. It wasn't the Green Berets. And he said, I don't know, that's what we were told. And all of this to me looked like some sort of coup and perhaps even the front-line could fall and the other side take over the town. I assumed that all of this might have been part of a game. It was quite senseless, but this was the last attempt of those paramilitaries to do something major of that kind. Fortunately, they were thwarted, and the situation was resolved to a large extent. And it should have been resolved before, but better late than never.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Did these events influence Goran Jelisic, and did he disappear from Brcko before or after this event? Do you know what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he left town long before this. I think he stopped turning up in town perhaps a month or a month and a half before this. Before this, some others came, because these bands and these paramilitaries didn't really like each other, and I think that he actually had to go away because he was afraid of a stronger unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the situation of the prison in Luka?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this prison was closed the same way it was opened. I really don't know, I couldn't tell you the dates, but they started taking people to Batkovici [Realtime transcript read in error "Batajnica"], which was a collection centre in Bijeljina, and I believe many people were taken there from that collection centre. And then sometime in June, I think -- well, I can't remember exactly when it was closed. I don't recall the details.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The name is Batkovici, not Batajnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Batkovici was a regular prison for prisoners of war under the supervision of the Red Cross; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I know about it. I was never there. I don't know who guarded that camp, but many people from Brcko were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement of 2011, on page 40, you say that the authorities did not conceal anything, that you demanded that records be kept of all those who were killed, and that this should be documented so that prosecutions could take place. You say on page 43 that: "When we found out that this was going on, we asked that the police identify each person and initiate the procedure. I don't know when the court in Brcko and the Prosecutor's Office were established, but some criminal reports were filed, and so on." Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, this is in line with what I said. This is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, let us now compare our tragic statistics. Would you say that the number of Serbs and non-Serbs killed in Brcko was balanced, more or less?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, recently some statistics were published, showing that these numbers were more or less equal. This is some sort of independent statistic showing how many people belonging to military units were killed, how many civilians. And according to these statistics, one might say that. Of course, we won't know the real situation until the lists of missing persons are put in order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. But from your statement in 2008, you were asked whether there was communication between the SDS and the War Presidency of Brcko at republican level, and you say there was no communication, that at Pale you contacted the government directly, the president of the Assembly, the prime minister of the president of the country, not the SDS. So if anything had to be done in writing, that was how it was done. I have to say that the role of the War Presidency made sense until the Executive Board was set up, the Executive Committee, and that's when the local government started functioning; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was the date I took to be the official date, although the 17th of May is the date when the War Presidency approved the programme of the new Executive Committee, and the decision was made in the afternoon. So we might consider that the 17th of May is the date, although the formation of the executive began on the next day, of the Executive Board.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. What did you say?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it time for a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a break for 45 minutes and resume at 1.35. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.49 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I take it that you do not have many items to cover now. You can conclude in half an hour? Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe even earlier. Can we now have 65 ter 7894. It's already admitted into evidence. Can we have 1D3878, please, 1D3878. Let's just take a glance at it in order to see how Brcko looked like and who got hold of it. 1D3878. I don't know if we have a Serbian version, but this is a Decree on District Military Courts in the Territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. Can we now turn to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that Brcko is included in the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna or, more specifically, the municipal of Ravno?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by this, the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May this be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What does it say about, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Excellency, I am accused of taking over Brcko. In fact, Brcko was divided into three municipalities, and everybody held to their part. And the Croatian part of the Brcko municipality was integrated into the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. That will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D1575, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 1D3879.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do we agree, Mr. Ristanic, that in Brcko there existed and was active, even before the blowing up of the bridge, the 108th Brigade of the HVO, and that the Croatian Army was deployed there even earlier?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, you see here on the 28th of October, weapons and ammunition and uniforms and boots are being sent to the 108th HVO Brigade deployed in Brcko; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1576, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 1D3869.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this a pass of the Brcko Garrison, Armed Forces of the Serbian Republic of BH, issued in the name of Mehmed Hodzic, allowing him to go to Germany with his ID on the 7th of July, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These kind of passes did exist.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Exhibit D1577.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have 1D3870. Serbian version, 72. This is a translation -- I mean page 2, that's the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is this a pass for Alma Fehartbegovic, allowing her to move around with her personal ID?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it's not clear. I see "MUP Krajina" here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. And the military post stamp is here?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Obviously, this is the military post using the preset form of the MUP Krajina, but the military post did affix their stamp.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Both are original, Mr. Hayden? The ERN numbers are different.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: I'll have to have a look at that and get back to you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have now 1D3872. Number 1 is the Serbian version and number 2 is the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, this one comes from the municipality of Brcko, 23rd of May, 1992. You issued a pass to a Muslim called Sidik Husic, ID card number 41/9/91?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: War Presidency of Brcko municipality, and this pass is allowing him to pass without being stopped?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was the purpose of a pass.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. These passes were provided to the OTP by the BiH government in 1995, and they came with the translation, the handwritten translations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. So there's no problem in admitting them in one exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. So 1D3870 shall be admitted Exhibit D1578, and 1D3872, Exhibit D1579.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Another document from this series is 1D3875, and I'm calling up this document because there's your signature on it. 1D3875. Is this your signature? On the 8th of May, you issue permission to Abdulah Muharemovic a pass allowing him to move within the municipality and out of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this is an identical form like the previous one, and this should be my signature. I think it is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1580, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is going to suffice.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ristanic, these passes were issued to everyone, except those who committed crimes?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, almost everybody who wanted to go out or move freely about could apply for a pass, except for those who were being investigated. You can see that the passes were issued by several different institutions; the MUP, the army, the municipality, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But was it easier for a Muslim to go out, because he had no obligation towards an army, than for a Serb, who had an obligation to the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs had problems in that respect because they had to seek permission and clearance from the army, and, as a rule, he had to give the pass back. But as I said, the military conscripts were issued with passes exclusively by the Draft Office and no one else.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May this be admitted? Oh, it's already been admitted. Can we now have 18430 -- 403, 18403.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether the translation has arrived, but you are going to help us, I hope. Do you see that this is dated the 18th of July, which is immediately before an action carried out by Davidovic and his specials.

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At the top, you see "SJB Brcko, Dragan Andan." We know who that is, because he's the one who was reporting from that area. He says that there are 170 police officers involved in combat, 40 of them from Lopare and 92 from Zvornik. Was that a major obstacle for carrying out regular police work?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it was, but this was a priority, and that is why they were re-subordinated to the army and deployed along the front-line.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: A little down in the letter, it says that in Semberija and Majevica, where there are no combat activities, the situation is pregnant and burdened with problems caused by plundering by paramilitary formations. Do you recall that this Mr. Andan was promoted to the position of acting chief of the Security Services Centre?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted for identification?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, this will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D1581, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ristanic, did you have information that rumours were circulating, and various misinformation or information, that the flats of retired army officers and prominent Serbs in Brcko were marked, as recommended by the Croatian minister of defence, Martin Spegelj, and they were marked for execution?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were cases like that, but not too many of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. One more question, Mr. Ristanic. Is it true that the Croatian Community occupied -- or, rather, took over their part of the municipality, the Muslims did the same with their part, and the Serbs did the same with their part, and that in Srpska Varos, which was traditionally a Serbian quarter, you did that because the barracks were close there; otherwise, you would have left the centre of the town?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. Initially, we did go, but we later returned because the barracks was there and there was enough manpower for the defence, and that is why we stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were there any such Muslim enclaves under our control, as they did with Cerik and Bukvik, who were in the Muslim territory? Were such Muslim enclaves situated in the Serbian part?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was only one, Brezovo Polje, some 14 to 15 kilometres from Brcko to Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And that is where they were arming themselves near the mosque and distributing weapons?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were rumours to that effect. The JNA established a company of Muslims, gave them arms, and they tasked them with guarding with the village in order to prevent escalation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please pause between questions and answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We didn't hear the answer of the witness to the last question. What was your answer, Mr. Ristanic? Because of the overlap, the interpreters couldn't hear your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that there was an enclave, Brezovo Polje, 14 kilometres from Brcko. There were rumours that the SDA tried to arm the population of that village. However, the JNA established a company made up exclusively of Muslims, gave them uniforms and weapons. I don't know exactly, but it remained there, as such, during a certain period of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can one say that the JNA only took care of who was in favour of it, rather than of the ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that that was the logic that they followed. It is well known that Brezovo Polje was practically an enclave and the people there were peaceful oriented. A lot of them worked in the merchant navy and they were known as people who were involved in boating and fishing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ristanic, did you feel that you had taken Brcko over from someone or do you feel that you only took control of what was Serbian?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we didn't have that former feeling. Practically in those first days, we didn't take away anything that belonged to someone else, because everybody took what belonged to them, as we thought was logical.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am very much grateful to you, and I apologise to you on behalf of the government which was unable to provide protection to you at the beginning of the war.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Mr. Ristanic, I have a few follow-up questions to today's cross-examination. Earlier today, at the beginning of the cross-examination, Mr. Karadzic took you to a line from Friday, in which you had said, with reference to Luka Camp, that: "He didn't listen to us." And Mr. Karadzic wanted to clarify whether you were referring to Mr. Jelisic or Mr. Veselic, and you said: "It was taken out of context, but I was basically referring to Veselic." This is at transcript page 5. I want to clarify now your relationship with Mr. Veselic and the police. First, who appointed Mr. Veselic to the position of chief of police?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And was that appointment confirmed by the Ministry of the Interior? I think we've spoken about this today. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And did you meet on a regular basis with Mr. Veselic in your capacity as president of the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Veselic was a member of that body, he was a member of the War Presidency, and we did meet. I'm not saying "regularly," but we did meet.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And did you issue instructions to Mr. Veselic, for example, with respect to Luka Camp and with respect to the ID'ing of deceased bodies that were collected by the sanitation services?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, that is the agreement reached by the War Presidency. It wasn't any kind of order. It was an agreement that was reached by the War Presidency, a conclusion that was reached by the War Presidency. And he was a member of that War Presidency, so that's exactly the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And did he implement those instructions or that agreement?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In certain parts, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And is it correct that the police, or persons, at least, in police uniform, were guarding Luka Camp?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: In light of the answers to the question I've just posed, can you explain what you meant when you said that Mr. Veselic did not listen to you or the War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't mean generally. I meant in terms of some of our individual positions, he didn't listen to us or obey us. He couldn't have obeyed because the circumstances were as they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: There was also a discussion today about the establishment of the Posavina corridor. This is at transcript page 22. And it was suggested, and you agreed, that the goal of establishing a corridor did not -- was not discussed, was not adopted, until wartime. Do you remember that discussion?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: In your amalgamated statement now in evidence, at Question 230, which is the final page of that statement, you discuss a trip to Sarajevo which occurred before May of 1992, in which you discussed certain maps and the objective of the Posavina corridor. And if I can take you to a similar reference in your interview of 2003. This is 65 ter 22238, page 19, please. And there's a reference there to this trip you made to Sarajevo, that you said you thought it was in February or March. You said that the leadership of the SDS was involved in those meetings, and you clarified that the leadership of the SDS included Radovan Karadzic, Momcilo Krajisnik - if we can turn the page to page 20 - and then you state, and this is in the middle of that page: "And the goal of that meeting was to find a territory through which it would be possible to make a corridor or connection to Krajina." Now, in light of that meeting in February or March 1992, was it the case that the goal of establishing the Posavina corridor was not contemplated until the conflict broke out?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Objection. This is misleading. It had been in the framework of conference, this Cutileiro Conference, not war objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness is here to testify, not Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Please, overruled, Mr. Karadzic. Have you finished your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Yes. The final question was: In light of the excerpt in the 2003 interview, was it really the case, as the witness stated today --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By the way, where do you have that passage on that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And on the page 20, and it's in the middle: "At that time ...," and the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Have you understood the question, Mr. Ristanic?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Are you able to answer?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have explained that. There were discussions, but in the context of peace. I just had a map once where the areas that were populated by Serbs were marked and where it was possible to establish some physical connection with parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina that we call Krajina. Excuse me, the area around Banja Luka, behind Doboj, we call that Krajina. So in peacetime conditions, because the strategic goals did not exist at that point in time, the aim of that discussion was that, or, actually, at the time I probably could not even remember Cutileiro or a peace plan. But probably in that ethnic division of Bosnia-Herzegovina in peacetime, that was the objective of that meeting, if that makes things a bit clearer now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Today there was discussion about events in Bukvik in September of 1992. This is at transcript page 44. There was a reference in one of your answers to the fact that Serbs who were moved out of Bukvik returned to Brcko to take revenge. Just to clarify, Mr. Ristanic, the reference to taking revenge is unrelated to the events in May and June of 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this is a poor interpretation. I did not say "revenge" anywhere, I did not use that expression. But never mind. These events from September have nothing to do with what happened in May 1992. These are things that happened as they did. There was this tragedy in Bukvik in September, and these people who were leaving had to be put up somewhere, and then they did certain things, sometimes even violent acts, in order to get into other people's apartments, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: You also provided evidence about your arrest in late July or maybe early August, as you stated at transcript page 62 onwards, and you provided a lengthy account of that arrest. I just wanted to clarify two things. The men who arrested you or the unit who arrested you, did they have anything to do with Luka Camp, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is hard to say from this distance, but perhaps some of them individually, in an indirect way, but I cannot be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And was their action of arresting you in any way related to steps that you may have taken with respect to either Luka Camp or other crimes committed in Brcko?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At any rate, no order suited these people. They functioned perfectly in chaos. That is when they were in power. Any kind of establishment of order kept them out, so that was probably one of the reasons. From the beginning of May until those days, we were constantly fighting, if I can put it that way, for the establishment of order. Then this unit came under Davidovic's command, and it was expected that they would do what they ultimately did, and this practically destroyed their world. They were no longer the rulers of Brcko, as it were.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Earlier today, you discussed the communication difficulties. This is at transcript pages 10 and 11. And you said, for example, that sometimes you would call and the person you were seeking was not in their office, and you had other difficulties in communicating with republic-level leaders. Do you recall that discussion?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: If we can go to page 118 of 65 ter 22238.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: In the 2003 interview, you discussed communications with Pale; in particular, Mr. Vojinovic's communication with persons such as Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Ostojic. And if we can turn to page -- if we look at the bottom of that excerpt there, you explain that you had immediate contacts, eye-to-eye meetings, rather than documenting your communication. Can you confirm that that was the case?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that I understand. Who did I talk to, who did I communicate with face to face?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: The interviewer in the 2003 interview asked you why this was not written down, your communication. And you answered, and I'll read the full answer because we don't have a B/C/S transcript: "Because the document that remains, and probably then an opinion which was like dominant, was like time will heal certain things and it will cover certain things from being. And I wasn't sure to whom I should address it to, whether it be used properly or abused. Therefore, we had immediate contacts, eye-to-eye meetings. And probably that's the reason why within this report," that was being discussed at the time, "there is nothing but the situation in general." The question is: Can you confirm that that was the case, that, in general, communication was eye-to-eye rather than through documents?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, certainly, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Turn the page to page 119.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Here, we see the reference to Mr. Vojinovic speaking most often with Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Ostojic, and you were asked: "And what, in particular, was he telling them about what was happening in Brcko?" And you answered: "I wasn't there, but from the things he told me and in later conversation when we went there together, he was straightforward, direct. He didn't wrap things, hide, concerning some other things, not this, but I am sure that this was also discussed." Can you confirm that that is your knowledge of the nature of Mr. Vojinovic's communications with Mr. Krajisnik and Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. It is being suggested here that there is knowledge involved, and the witness said that that is what he believes. He said that he was not there, and his conclusion is that it was that way because Dr. Beli was there. The Prosecutor cannot put leading questions like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it your knowledge -- could you reformulate the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: There's no suggestion here, Mr. President, that it was Mr. Ristanic conducting this communication. I'm inquiring about what he knows of Mr. Vojinovic's communications. Mr. Vojinovic is now deceased, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. You can ask --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- in that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: You've heard the excerpt from the interview, Mr. Ristanic. Can you confirm that that was what you knew about Mr. Vojinovic's communication with Pale?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew about those communications through Mr. Vojinovic, that is to say, when the two of us talked, because, in a way, we were the most responsible persons there and we were affected by these problems the most. That is why we drafted this together, what he should point out when he sees these people. Then, as far as I can remember from this time distance, I had the impression that he did talk about all of those things to those persons. Now, how convincingly, and how much time he had available, and how seriously he was taken, time will show that. And time did show that ultimately there was an intervention, but probably when conditions were created for that, probably a bit too late.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ristanic. No more questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Ristanic, just one question from me. You remember you had a discussion with Mr. Karadzic about the Variant A and B document. It's at transcript page 16, line 7 -- or 6 to 8. Do you remember having said this, I quote: "Our assessment was that what can be done should be done, and what cannot be done should not be done by force"?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And that answer was followed by the question from Mr. Karadzic, I quote: "Do you then agree that this document, unlike other party decisions, was optional, so those who wanted to could implement things, but those who did not want to would not be subject to any pressuring or sanctions from the party?" And you answered to this effect. At one point in time, you say: "It probably did not contain anything referring to consequences of failure to implement it." And later on, you also said: "If something was agreed on at the top, we would implement it. Otherwise, we wouldn't, because nothing could remain secret." Do you remember that discussion?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So I was not clear whether this was -- to implement the document was discretional on the part of each war presidency or each municipality. Moreover, when you read out the paragraph -- or Question 35 in your amalgamated statement, you said to this effect, I read -- I will quote: "So things were never discussed with some arguments, arguments or something, because if it was the opinion of the president, then it was like Holy Grail. It shouldn't be -- it was quite authoritative." So having heard all these discussion and your statement, could you expand on the issue as to whether that document, Variant A and B, was of a mandatory nature or otherwise, if you could?

utterances.speaker: DJORDJE RISTANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it pertains to two periods. I spoke about the time before the conflict broke out, that is to say, the debates within the party about Variant A and Variant B. I said then that no one bore any responsibility if this would not be fully carried through, and that's the way it was. But when I said that the president's word was respected, I meant the local president of the Serb Democratic Party. From the more extensive statement, you will see that it pertained to him. This man did not explain much, he did not talk much, but he decided things the way he did, and we basically went by that. I never said "Holy Grail." That is the translation that was put there. But I think I must have said "Holy Writ," but it must be another word that would have been the authentic word used at that time, but it boils down to the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ristanic. That concludes your evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I? Maybe when the witness leaves, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is it, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I didn't manage to tender those three documents, those three statements, 65 ter 22237, 22238 and 23193, that is 1998, 2003, 2011.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In their entirety, Mr. Karadzic, or those pages you dealt with?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it would be better in their entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: No objection from us, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm concerned about being inundated with a lot of documents. All relevant parts were read and put to the witness. Do you really need those documents?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I put certain things in my own words, I did not read them verbatim, so perhaps those pages from where I read this out, or, rather, recounted what was written there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So shall we admit them for reference purposes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: I guess that makes sense, bearing in mind that the 1998 and 2003 interviews are essentially the amalgamated statement or large chunks thereof.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we'll do that, we'll admit them for references -- reference purposes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we give them numbers?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. They will be admitted as Exhibits D1582 through 1584 respectively, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. On behalf of the Chamber and the Tribunal, as a whole, Mr. Ristanic, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague again to give it. Please have a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is the next witness ready?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask for a change in my own team?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we have a break for five minutes? Yes. We'll resume at half past. --- Break taken at 2.24 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, if you could make -- introduce your team.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. You already know Mr. Aleksandar Vujic, and with me, thanks to your kind decision, is my advisor for military issues, General Radovan Radinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Radinovic. Yes, Mr. Uertz-Retzlaff.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir, Mr. Theunens.

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Could you please state your full name?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: My name is Reynaud Theunens.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And, Mr. Theunens, did you provide a CV to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, I did, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Can we please have Exhibit 65 ter 11703 brought up onto the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, is that the CV that you provided?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours, this is the CV I provided before my departure from the OTP of the ICTY in April of 2009.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you said you left the ICTY, and what is your current position? What are you doing nowadays?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, since April 2009, I am the chief of the Joint Mission Analysis Centre in the UNIFIL Mission in Lebanon, so the UN interim force in Lebanon.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: From your CV, we see that you worked in the Military Analyst Team from 2001 onwards. And while working in this MAT, Military Analyst Team, did your research and analysis cover military activities of various military fractions involved in the conflict in the former Yugoslavia or just one?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Your Honours, my professional activities in the MAT at the OTP from June 2001 to April 2009 covered JNA, i.e., SFRY armed forces, local Serb forces in Croatia, local Serb forces in Bosnia-Herzegovina, as well as ZNG and HV, I mean, so the Croatian forces in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In footnote 2 -- can we see a little bit more of the CV? A bit further down. We need to see the lower part.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: In footnote 2, you indicate that you testified in several cases, and you specify the cases, until summer 2006. Did you testify before this Tribunal after that?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honours. I'm just checking the footnote. But after that, I also testified in the trial of Mr. Vojislav Seselj, in the trial of Ante Gotovina, Mladen Markac and Ivan Cermak. I also testified in an Appeals Hearing of Mr. Veselin Sljivancanin. And my last testimony was last year, in October, in the trial of Mr. Jovica Stanisic and Mr. Frenki -- or, Franko - excuse me - Simatovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And did you always testify as an expert?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, I request the CV to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be done.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3031, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Mr. Theunens, you provided a report "Radovan Karadzic and the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, TO and VRS, 1992 to 1995," dated 15 April 2009 to the Office of the Prosecutor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And you also provided an addendum and a corrigendum to this report; is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: At the end of your report, in a separate document you detail the scope and the methodology of your work when producing the report. In particular, in paragraph 3, you refer to the intelligence cycle, a method that you applied. Can you explain to the Court what that entails?

utterances.speaker: REYNAUD THEUNENS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. The intelligence cycle overall includes four discrete phases. "Discrete" means that the four phases are conducted simultaneously or can be conducted simultaneously. These four phases are: direction, collection, processing and dissemination, whereby processing consists of five steps, and some of them, again, are conducted simultaneously.
